prompt: How do you cancel the order ord-1001 in boxoffice?
hint: The address names the thing; the method says what to do with it.

choices.text: POST /v1/orders/ord-1001/cancel
choices.why: That puts a verb in the path, the function-name picture of an API; boxoffice has no such address.

choices.text: DELETE /v1/orders/ord-1001
choices.why: Right. The order is a resource at its own address, and DELETE is the verb.

choices.text: GET /v1/cancelOrder?id=ord-1001
choices.why: A GET must not change anything, and the path names an action rather than a resource.

choices.text: PUT /v1/orders/ord-1001 with a body saying the status is cancelled
choices.why: Some APIs work that way; boxoffice's table of addresses gives PUT to nothing.

prompt: You read ord-1001 with a token and get 200. The next request, to the same address from the same terminal, carries no token. What does boxoffice answer?
hint: What does the server keep between two requests?

choices.text: 200, since it recognises the client of the request before
choices.why: That is the logged-in website picture; boxoffice keeps no memory of the conversation.

choices.text: 200 until the token's fifteen minutes run out
choices.why: The token's life only matters for requests that carry it; this one carries nothing.

choices.text: 401, no bearer token
choices.why: Right. Each request is judged on what it carries, and this one carries no credentials.

choices.text: 404, because without a token the order does not exist
choices.why: boxoffice checks the token first and answers 401 before it looks for the order.

prompt: Why does statelessness make an API easier to test than a sequence of screens?
hint: What does the answer to a request depend on?

choices.text: A request stands alone, and its answer depends only on it and the data
choices.why: Right. No earlier request has to be replayed to reach the state a test needs.

choices.text: The server forgets its data between requests, so no test can affect another
choices.why: The server forgets the conversation, not the data: an order created stays created, which is lesson 12's problem.

choices.text: Nothing is stored, so every answer comes back faster
choices.why: Speed is not what statelessness buys a test; independence is.

choices.text: After the first request, a test no longer needs a token
choices.why: The opposite: every request needs its token, because nothing carries over.

prompt: A test runs `jq '.payment == null'` on an order to prove that the order has no payment field. What is wrong with that test?
hint: Run it on an order where the field exists with the value null.

choices.text: jq raises an error when a field is missing, so the test crashes
choices.why: jq answers null for a missing field, quietly; that is the trouble.

choices.text: Missing and null are the same thing in JSON
choices.why: They are different: one says nothing was sent, the other says the value is empty.

choices.text: It passes for a field present with null too
choices.why: Right. Only `has("payment")` tells the two cases apart.

choices.text: jq compares null only with ===, which it does not have
choices.why: jq's == compares null correctly; the comparison works, it just asks the wrong question.

prompt: In JSON a field that is ___ has not been sent at all, which is not the same as a field sent with the value null.
hint: The opposite of present.

prompt: An order is for 3 seats of sh-103, whose price_cents is 6500. What should its total_cents be?
hint: Whole cents, multiplied.

prompt: An API sends `"starts_at": "2026-11-08T18:00:00"`, with no offset. An app on a phone set to UTC and one on a phone set to São Paulo time both show it. What happens?
hint: Section 03 read the same text under two values of TZ.

choices.text: Both treat it as São Paulo time, since that is where the theatre is
choices.why: Nothing in the text says São Paulo; each phone fills in its own zone.

choices.text: Both refuse it, because ISO 8601 requires an offset
choices.why: ISO 8601 allows a local time with no offset; the parse succeeds, and that is the danger.

choices.text: Both read it as UTC and agree
choices.why: That was not what happened in section 03: the reading depended on the machine's zone.

choices.text: They read two moments three hours apart
choices.why: Right. Without an offset, the same text means a different instant on each machine.

prompt: Another API sends order ids as numbers, such as 9007199254740993, and its JavaScript app keeps opening order 9007199254740992. What fixes it at the source?
hint: What can a JavaScript number hold exactly?

choices.text: Declare the id as a 64-bit integer in the JSON
choices.why: JSON has no integer types to declare; every number is just a number, and the app still reads floating point.

choices.text: Send the id as a JSON string
choices.why: Right. A string is never converted to a number, so no digit can change.

choices.text: Have the app add one to every id it receives
choices.why: That fixes one id by luck and breaks every id that was exact.

choices.text: Send it with a decimal point, as 9007199254740993.0
choices.why: 2.0 and 2 are the same JSON number; the decimal point changes nothing about precision.

prompt: Why does boxoffice send prices as `"price_cents": 8000` rather than `"price": 80.00`?
hint: What did 80.10 times 3 print?

choices.text: JSON cannot carry a decimal point
choices.why: It can: 0.1 is valid JSON. The trouble is how it is read.

choices.text: Whole cents are exact, and fractions of reais read as binary floating point are not
choices.why: Right. 80.10 times 3 came out as 240.29999999999998.

choices.text: A whole number takes fewer bytes on the network
choices.why: 8000 and 80.00 are about the same size; size is not the reason.

choices.text: The bank that takes the payments refuses decimals
choices.why: boxoffice charges locally in the lab; the choice is about arithmetic, not a bank's rule.

prompt: openapi.yaml says unknown fields are refused, and boxoffice accepts them. What does a tester conclude?
hint: Who decides which one is wrong?

choices.text: The code is right, because the code is what runs
choices.why: Then every test would pass forever; the contract is what was promised.

choices.text: One of the two is wrong, and the disagreement is a finding to report
choices.why: Right. The team may fix the code or the document; the tester's job is to make the disagreement visible.

choices.text: Nothing, since documents always lag behind code
choices.why: That is the belief the section asks you to drop: a lagging contract is itself a defect.

choices.text: The document is right, so the code is a defect
choices.why: Sometimes the document is the one that is wrong; the team decides, with the finding in front of it.

prompt: Match each part of openapi.yaml to what it holds.
hint: The section's walk through the order operation.

pairs.right: every address, and what each method does there
the answers allowed, keyed by status code
what the client may send in the body

prompt: An endpoint answers 500 to a request the contract describes, and the body is a perfectly shaped Problem. Does the answer honour the contract?
hint: Is the shape of the body the whole promise?

choices.text: Yes, because the body has every field Problem requires
choices.why: The shape is half the promise; the status code has to be one the operation lists.

choices.text: No: 500 is not among the codes it lists
choices.why: Right. A code missing from the list is one the client was told it would never see.

choices.text: Yes: every contract allows a 5xx whenever the server fails
choices.why: This one lists 502 and 504 for the payment provider, and no 500 anywhere.

choices.text: Only if its detail explains what failed
choices.why: detail is for people; it cannot make an unlisted code a listed one.

prompt: Which fields of a problem details body should a program decide on?
hint: Which ones are written for people?

choices.text: status
choices.why: Right. It repeats the status code inside the body.

choices.text: type
choices.why: Right. It names the kind of problem, for programs to tell kinds apart.

choices.text: detail
choices.why: It is a sentence for a person, and its wording will change one day.

choices.text: title
choices.why: A short summary for people; programs should use the type it summarises.

prompt: A test checks that every response's content-type starts with `application/json`. What happens when it runs against boxoffice's errors?
hint: Section 05 printed the label with curl's -w.

choices.text: It passes, because problem+json is a kind of JSON
choices.why: It is JSON, but the text `application/problem+json` does not start with `application/json`.

choices.text: It fails only on the token endpoint
choices.why: The token endpoint is the one place errors are labelled application/json.

choices.text: It fails on the problem errors
choices.why: Right. They say application/problem+json, and the check should accept that label.

choices.text: It fails on every response, errors and successes alike
choices.why: Successful answers are labelled application/json and pass.

prompt: The token endpoint answers `{"error":"invalid_client"}`, not problem details. Is that a defect?
hint: Which standard governs that endpoint, and what does the contract say?

choices.text: No: OAuth prescribes that shape there, and the contract says so
choices.why: Right. A second shape is fine when it is documented; OAuth client libraries expect this one.

choices.text: Yes: every error of an API must follow RFC 9457
choices.why: RFC 9457 is a choice an API makes; OAuth's token endpoint has its own required shape.

choices.text: Yes, because it is labelled application/json
choices.why: That label matches its body exactly; the label is not the problem.

choices.text: No, since an endpoint may answer errors in any shape
choices.why: An undocumented shape would be a defect; this one is fine because it is written down.

prompt: The contract says seats is an integer from 1 to 6. Which of these values are boundary cases for that rule?
hint: The values on each side of each edge.

choices.why: Right: just below the lowest valid value.
Right: the lowest valid value.
A fine value for the valid class, and on no edge.
Right: the highest valid value.
Right: just above the highest valid value.
That is the size of the show, a different rule; for this one it is just another value above 6.

prompt: boxoffice answered `{"show_id":"sh-101","seats":2.0}` with 201. What should the report say?
hint: How many numbers are 2 and 2.0 in JSON?

choices.text: Defect: a decimal was accepted where the contract says integer
choices.why: 2.0 is not a decimal in any sense JSON knows; it is the number 2, which the rule allows.

choices.text: Nothing: it is the integer 2
choices.why: Right. The case passed, and reporting it would cost credibility.

choices.text: Defect: it should have answered 400, because the body is malformed
choices.why: The body is valid JSON; 400 is for a body that cannot be read at all.

choices.text: Defect: the reply shows seats as 2, not as the 2.0 that was sent
choices.why: Both spell the same number, so the reply did not change the value.

prompt: Put the steps from a contract clause to a defect report in order.
hint: The expected answer comes before the request is sent.
items: read a clause of the contract
derive the cases it gives, each with its expected answer
compare each answer with the one expected
write up the request, the answer, the clause and the transcript

prompt: boxoffice ignored the price_cents field it was sent and charged the real price. Why is accepting the field silently still a risk?
hint: Think about the program that sent it.

choices.text: A later version of boxoffice may charge the price the client sent
choices.why: That would be a different defect; the risk exists today, with the code as it is.

choices.text: The extra field makes the JSON invalid
choices.why: The JSON is valid; only the contract forbids the field.

choices.text: Each unknown field slows the server down
choices.why: An ignored field costs nothing measurable; the risk is a misunderstanding.

choices.text: The client believes its field was obeyed
choices.why: Right. A 201 tells it everything went through, including what was ignored.

prompt: The body `null` got a 500 whose body carried no stack trace. A colleague says that makes the answer acceptable. What do you reply?
hint: Section 05 listed four checks for an error, in order.

choices.text: Agreed: an error that leaks nothing meets the contract
choices.why: Not leaking is the fourth check; the first, the status code, already failed.

choices.text: The leak check passed, and the code check failed: it should be a 4xx
choices.why: Right. A 500 blames the server for a client's mistake and invites a useless retry.

choices.text: Agreed, because null is not valid JSON, so any answer will do
choices.why: null is a complete, valid JSON document; it is just not an object.

choices.text: Disagreed: the body should have carried the trace, to help the client
choices.why: The trace belongs in the server's log; sending it to clients is the leak the fourth check forbids.

prompt: A new endpoint takes `?row=` with a letter from A to P. Following section 06, which set of cases do you send for row?
hint: Edges, the wrong kind of value, and the parameter left out.

choices.text: Every letter from A to P, one request each
choices.why: Sixteen cases in one class, and none outside it: the edges are where limits break.

choices.text: A and P only, since the rest behave alike
choices.why: Those are the valid edges; the values just outside them, and the wrong kinds, are missing.

choices.text: A, P, the letters just outside them, a digit, and no row
choices.why: Right. Both edges from each side, a value of the wrong kind, and the parameter missing.

choices.text: A random letter on each run, so that over time all are covered
choices.why: A test whose input changes every run cannot be compared from one run to the next, and it skips the edges.

prompt: Match each case from section 06 to what it showed.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.right: an empty 200 where the contract says 400

prompt: A test of `GET /v1/orders/ord-1001` passes when it runs after the other tests and fails when it runs first, on a freshly started boxoffice. Which statement explains it?
hint: Statelessness is about the conversation. What else does the server hold?

choices.text: boxoffice remembers the token of the test that ran before
choices.why: No request inherits anything from the one before; the token has to be in every request.

choices.text: The order exists only if an earlier request created it
choices.why: Right. Statelessness covers the conversation, not the data; lesson 12 deals with tests that share data.

choices.text: A REST API answers differently depending on the order of requests
choices.why: Its answers depend on the data, not on the order; the order matters here only because of what got created.

choices.text: The first request after a restart is always refused
choices.why: A fresh boxoffice answers its first request like any other; what is missing is the order.
